sermon:
## The Charge and the Foremost Sinner
*Why the law was never meant to make you clever*

**Text:** 1 Timothy 1:1–20 · **Supporting:** Galatians 3:24; Romans 7:7; 1 Corinthians 15:9–10; Luke 18:13

A young pastor is standing in front of a problem he did not create and cannot ignore. Paul left him in Ephesus for one reason, and the letter opens by naming it without ceremony. There are men in that church who have made the Scriptures into a hobby. They are impressive. They are confident. And they are killing the people they are supposed to feed.

**The teaching that flatters and the law that exposes**
Paul does not ease into it. "As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus, when I went into Macedonia, that thou mightest charge some that they teach no other doctrine, neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith." (1 Timothy 1:3–4) Notice what the false teachers are doing. They are not denying the law. They are decorating it. They have turned the holy text into a maze of speculation, a sport for the clever, a way to seem deep while never once being undone. Paul calls it what it is: "desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm." (1 Timothy 1:7)

This is the oldest substitution in the church. Take the word that was given to break you and use it to build yourself a reputation. The law becomes an occasion for cleverness instead of an occasion for repentance. And Paul will not have it, because he knows what the law is actually for. "The law is good, if a man use it lawfully." (1 Timothy 1:8) Its job is not to give the comfortable a new subject to master. Its job is to drag the murderer, the liar, the proud man, "and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine" (1 Timothy 1:10) into the light and leave him with nowhere to stand. The law is the schoolmaster, as Paul told the Galatians, that brings us to Christ. "Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith." (Galatians 3:24) It was never the destination. It was the thing that ran us out of options.

Paul knew that personally. "I had not known sin, but by the law," he wrote to the Romans; "for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet." (Romans 7:7) The law did not make him righteous. It made him aware. It held up a mirror and showed him a man he could not fix, and that is exactly the work the Ephesian teachers had defused. They had taken the mirror and turned it into a kaleidoscope, endless patterns, fables, genealogies, a thousand fascinating things to look at, and not one of them his own face. A law that no longer convicts has been disarmed, however much of it you can recite.

I have used the Bible to look smart. I have stood over a text and felt the small heat of mastering it, and never once let it master me. That is the false teacher's instinct, and it lives in the pulpit as easily as in the pew.

**The witness who is himself the evidence**
Then the letter turns, and it turns onto the writer. Paul has been describing dangerous men, and now he tells you the most dangerous man in the letter is the one holding the pen. "And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who hath enabled me, for that he counted me faithful, putting me into the ministry; who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious." (1 Timothy 1:12–13) He does not soften it. He had hunted the church. He had approved the killing. He told the Corinthians the same thing without flinching: "For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God." (1 Corinthians 15:9)

And here is the sentence the whole letter rests on. "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief." (1 Timothy 1:15) Read it slowly. Not *was* chief, back before the conversion cleaned him up. *Am.* Present tense. The apostle, years into the ministry, books into the canon, still calls himself the worst man in the room. This is not false modesty. It is the only ground a minister can stand on. Paul says he was shown mercy for a reason: "that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting." (1 Timothy 1:16) He is Exhibit A. If the patience of Christ reached the man holding the coats at Stephen's stoning, there is no one it cannot reach.

**The mercy that does the silencing**
Watch how the chapter ends, because Paul does something the false teachers never could. He hands two men over. "Of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme." (1 Timothy 1:20) That is severe. But the severity comes from the same place the mercy did. Paul disciplines because he was disciplined by grace, not by argument. The clever teachers in Ephesus could win debates. They could not save anyone. They had a law without a Savior, knowledge without a wound, and a religion that left them exactly as proud as it found them.

The tax collector in Luke's gospel did not have a system. He had eight words. "God be merciful to me a sinner." (Luke 18:13) And Jesus said that man went home justified, and the expert did not. The difference between sound doctrine and dangerous doctrine is not how much you know. It is whether what you know has ever brought you to your knees.

So before this letter tells a church how to pray, how to choose its leaders, how to honor its widows and fight its fight, it tells you the one thing under all of it. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. The foremost of them is writing the instructions. And if you have read this far feeling steady about where you stand, the law has not finished with you yet.

Mercy found the worst of us.

## Prayer First, and the One Mediator
*What a church does before it does anything else*

**Text:** 1 Timothy 2:1–15 · **Supporting:** 1 Timothy 2:5–6; Ezekiel 18:23; John 14:6; Matthew 5:44

Ask a church to describe its priorities and you will get a list. Worship, teaching, missions, the building fund, the next event. Paul, telling a church under pressure what comes first, says something we would never have written. Before anything. Before strategy, before defense, before the thing that feels urgent. Pray. And not for yourselves.

**The word "first," and who it is aimed at**
"I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; for kings, and for all that are in authority." (1 Timothy 2:1–2) First of all. Not first in the bulletin. First in weight. And then the direction of the prayer should stop us, because it runs exactly opposite to instinct. *Kings.* *All that are in authority.* This church was a tiny minority under an empire that would, within a generation, learn to burn Christians for sport. Paul does not tell them to pray against Rome. He tells them to pray for it.

That is not politics. It is theology. "For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth." (1 Timothy 2:3–4) The church prays for all people because God's posture toward all people is mercy held out, not vengeance withheld. He said it through Ezekiel centuries before: "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord God: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23) A church that only prays for itself has quietly decided that the people outside the room are enemies first and image-bearers second. Jesus closed that door. "Pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you." (Matthew 5:44) The Ephesian believers were to pray for the men who might one day arrest them. So are we, for the people we have decided are the problem.

I have led a church in prayer and prayed almost entirely for us. Our needs, our growth, our protection. The world outside the walls came up as a threat to be survived, not a field God loves. That is not the prayer Paul put first.

**The single bridge across an infinite gap**
Now Paul gives the reason underneath the reason, and it is the doctrinal center of the whole letter. "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time." (1 Timothy 2:5–6) One God. One mediator. One. Not a system of intermediaries, not a hierarchy of saints and priests you climb like a ladder, not your own sincerity offered up as a bridge. One man stands in the gap, and he stands there because he closed it with his own body.

A mediator is someone who can put a hand on both parties at once. To touch God, he had to be God. To touch us, he had to be a man, and Paul says it precisely, "the man Christ Jesus." He gave himself a ransom. A ransom is a price paid to free a captive who cannot free himself. This is why the church prays for all men: because the ransom was offered for all, the door is genuinely open, and there is exactly one door. "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." (John 14:6) The exclusivity of Christ is not a wall the church builds. It is the only bridge, and it is wide enough for the world.

Sit with the words Paul chose. *Between God and men.* He is naming a distance, a holy God on one side and guilty men on the other, and a gap no amount of religion has ever bridged from below. The false teachers in Ephesus were, in their own way, gap-closers. Their rules, their pedigrees, their endless mastery of the law were all ladders leaned against the wall of heaven, and every one of them was too short. Paul says the gap was closed from the other side, by one man, at the price of himself. *He gave himself.* Not a contribution toward the ransom. The whole of it. And that single fact reorders how a church prays, because if Christ is the one mediator then no one is beyond the reach of his mediation, not the emperor, not the persecutor, not the man you have privately written off. To pray only for our own is to act as though the ransom had a smaller scope than the cross.

**Worship that adorns the gospel instead of distracting from it**
So when Paul turns to how men and women conduct themselves in the gathered church, the men praying "without wrath and doubting" (1 Timothy 2:8), the women adorned "with good works" rather than spectacle (1 Timothy 2:9–10), he is not changing subjects. He is asking one question of the assembly: does our conduct point at the one mediator, or at ourselves? The men full of anger and argument, the worshiper turning the gathering into a display of status, both pull the eye off Christ and onto the performer. The hardest verses in this chapter (1 Timothy 2:11–15) sit inside that single concern: a worshiping people whose order, in the household of the gospel, adorns the message instead of competing with it.

A church can do everything else and miss this. It can be busy, defended, full of opinion, and never once get on its knees for the people it is sure are the enemy. The cross was not offered for the people who deserved it. It was offered for the man who held the coats, for the king on the throne, for the neighbor you cannot stand. There is one mediator, and he gave himself a ransom for all. The question that should follow you out of the room is simpler than you want it to be. Whose name came up when you prayed this week, and whose didn't?

One mediator. Pray for all.

## Character Before Office
*Why the church measures the man, not the résumé*

**Text:** 1 Timothy 3:1–16 · **Supporting:** 1 Timothy 3:15; Titus 1:7–9; Acts 20:28; Matthew 7:16

Every other institution in the world hires for competence. Can he do the job. Can he close the deal, win the room, grow the numbers. The church Paul is describing measures something almost no one else measures, and it measures it first. Not what a man can do. What a man is. And the list he gives the young pastor is, at almost every point, not a list of skills.

**A list with one ability and a wall of character**
"This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work." (1 Timothy 3:1) Good. Wanting to lead is not pride. But then read what qualifies the desire. "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach; not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous; one that ruleth well his own house." (1 Timothy 3:2–4)

Count the abilities on that list. One. "Apt to teach." Everything else is character. Self-controlled. Not violent. Not a drunk. Not greedy. Gentle. Not quarrelsome. Faithful at home. Paul is doing something deliberate and almost offensive to the modern ear: he is saying the question of whether a man should lead the church is overwhelmingly a question of who he is when no one is watching, and only marginally a question of what he can perform when everyone is. He told Titus the same thing in the same breath, "For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God" (Titus 1:7), a steward, a man trusted with what belongs to another.

And he plants a test inside the list that no platform can fake. "One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (for if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?)" (1 Timothy 3:4–5) The home is the proving ground. Not because a man's children are robots he controls, but because the home is the one place he cannot perform his way through. The church is going to find out who he is. Better that it find out before, in the small kingdom, than after, in the larger one.

I have wanted the office more than I have wanted the character it requires. I have measured myself by what I could do in front of a room and quietly skipped the harder audit of who I am behind a door. Paul will not let me. The office requires the man.

**Tested first, then trusted**
Watch the verb Paul uses for the deacons, because it is the whole doctrine in one word. "And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless." (1 Timothy 3:10) Proved. Tested. Tried over time. Not interviewed once and installed. The church is not looking for a man who can pass an inspection on a chosen day. It is looking for a man who has been watched across years and "found blameless", found, the way you find what was always there. Jesus gave the church its testing instrument: "Ye shall know them by their fruits." (Matthew 7:16) Fruit takes a season. It cannot be manufactured for a meeting.

This is why a church should be patient and a little slow about its leaders, and almost never impressed by speed. The gifted newcomer, the man who arrives fully formed and dazzling, Paul flags him directly: "Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil." (1 Timothy 3:6) Charisma is not character. It can even be its counterfeit, the very thing that lets a man skip the testing. The church that hands a man authority because he is gifted, before it knows whether he is godly, has misread the entire chapter.

**The house, the pillar, and the mystery at the center**
Why does any of this matter so much? Paul stops and tells you, and it is the reason the standards are this high. "That thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth." (1 Timothy 3:15) The church is not a club. It is the household of God and the pillar that holds the truth up where the world can see it. Leaders are not running an organization. They are guarding a deposit. Paul charged the Ephesian elders to "feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood." (Acts 20:28) Purchased with blood. That is the price tag on the thing these men are handling.

And then, lest a single overseer read this and think the standard is something he generates, the chapter ends not on the man but on the mystery the man is meant to embody. "And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory." (1 Timothy 3:16) There is the standard, and there is the only one who ever met it. The character Paul demands of leaders is the character of Christ, who was everything this chapter asks and gave himself for men who are not. No overseer embodies the mystery on his own strength. He embodies it the way a window embodies light, by letting it through, and getting out of the way.

So the church measures the man. Not because the man is the point, but because a leader who has not been broken and remade by the gospel will hand the people something other than the gospel, and call it leadership.

The office requires the man.

## Train Yourself for Godliness
*The difference between forbidding and feeding*

**Text:** 1 Timothy 4:1–16 · **Supporting:** 1 Timothy 4:7–8; Genesis 1:31; Colossians 2:20–23; 1 Corinthians 9:27

There is a kind of false religion that does not look like indulgence. It looks like discipline. It forbids and abstains and denies, and it wears its restrictions like medals. Paul saw it coming into the Ephesian church, and the strange thing is how holy it looked while it was poisoning people.

**The lie that comes dressed as holiness**
"Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils." (1 Timothy 4:1) Doctrines of devils, and then Paul tells you what these particular devils were teaching. Not debauchery. Restriction. "Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving." (1 Timothy 4:3) The false teachers were not telling people to sin. They were telling people that God's good gifts were the problem. Marriage, food, the body, call them dirty, deny them, and you will be spiritual.

Paul cuts it down with the first page of the Bible. "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." (1 Timothy 4:4) When God finished the world, "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." (Genesis 1:31) You do not get more spiritual by despising what God called very good. Paul made the same argument to the Colossians and named the trap exactly: these rules "have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh." (Colossians 2:23) A show of wisdom. That is the danger. The thing looked like devotion and was actually a way of earning what cannot be earned, a religion of subtraction where the gospel is a religion of grace.

**Forbidding is easy; training is the work**
So Paul gives the minister the opposite instruction, and the contrast is the heart of the chapter. The false teachers forbid. The good minister feeds and trains. "Nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine" (1 Timothy 4:6), nourished, fed, the language of a meal, not a fast. And then the command the whole letter turns on: "But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness. For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come." (1 Timothy 4:7–8)

*Exercise thyself.* Train. The word is the one Paul borrows from the athlete, the gymnasium, the years of unglamorous repetition. He used it on himself: "But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway." (1 Corinthians 9:27) Godliness is not a mood that descends on you. It is a thing you train toward, the way a runner trains, in a thousand small invisible disciplines that no one applauds. And here is what makes this gospel and not law: the forbidding religion was trying to *become* acceptable. The training Paul commands starts from a man already accepted, and works out the godliness that grace has already planted. One is climbing. The other is growing.

I have preferred the rule to the training, because the rule is finished by lunch and the training is never finished at all. It is far easier to forbid a thing than to be slowly remade. The man who builds a wall of prohibitions can feel holy by Tuesday. The man training for godliness will still be at it on his last day. I know which one I have reached for.

**Watch your life and your teaching, both, and closely**
Then Paul does what he keeps doing in this letter: he turns the charge onto the minister himself, and refuses to let him hide behind his office. "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity." (1 Timothy 4:12) Be the thing you teach. And then the verse that should hang over every pulpit. "Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee." (1 Timothy 4:16)

Both. Thyself, and the doctrine. Watch your life and watch your teaching, and watch them with equal care, because a man can get the doctrine flawless and let the life rot, and the rot will preach louder than the truth. Paul will not let a minister separate the two. The message and the messenger travel together. A church does not only hear what its leaders say. It watches what they are, and over time it becomes what they are far more than what they say.

This is the mercy hiding inside the hard command. The training, the example, the watching, none of it is a ladder up to God. The minister trains for godliness because Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and the saved sinner spends the rest of his life being made to match the salvation he did not earn. You are not training to be accepted. You were accepted, and now you train. The athlete in the gospel runs because the prize is already his.

So refuse the religion that only knows how to forbid. It feels like holiness and it ends in pride. Be fed instead. Be trained. And watch your life as closely as your doctrine, because the people who hear you are watching both, and so is the One who saved you.

Train yourself. Watch your life.

## Honor in the Household of God
*A church that runs on justice, not preference*

**Text:** 1 Timothy 5:1–25 · **Supporting:** 1 Timothy 5:8; James 1:27; Deuteronomy 25:4; Galatians 6:10

There is a test for whether a church actually believes the gospel, and it is not the doctrinal statement on the website. It is how the church treats the people who cannot pay it back. The widow with no family. The elder no one is watching anymore. The member nobody likes. Paul spends a whole chapter here, and it is the least quoted in the letter, because it is about the unglamorous machinery of justice inside a family.

**Family first, then the church**
Paul opens by setting the temperature of the whole community. "Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren; the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity." (1 Timothy 5:1–2) The church is not a corporation with clients. It is a family, and you speak to family differently than you speak to strangers or staff. Hold that, because everything that follows is family logic.

Then he gets specific about widows, and he does something that cuts against the soft assumption that the church should simply absorb every need. He pushes the responsibility back onto the family first. "But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God." (1 Timothy 5:4) And then the hardest sentence in the chapter. "But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel." (1 Timothy 5:8) Worse than an unbeliever. The man who lets the church carry a burden his own family should carry has not been generous to the church. He has denied the faith. Pure religion is not a feeling. James said it plainly: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." (James 1:27) Provision is not optional charity. It is the faith, working.

I have been quick to let an institution carry what I was supposed to carry myself. It is easy to be generous with the church's resources and stingy with my own obligations, and to feel righteous doing it. Paul names that move and calls it a denial.

**Honor that costs something, and judgment that waits for evidence**
Then Paul turns to the elders, and notice he ties justice to honor with a verse pulled straight out of Moses. "Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine. For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward." (1 Timothy 5:17–18) The ox that does the work gets to eat. The man who labors in the word gets honored and supported, in dignity and in pay. A church that runs its leaders into the ground and calls it humility has muzzled the ox and quoted Scripture while doing it.

But honor does not mean immunity, and here Paul is just. Elders are to be protected from gossip, "against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses" (1 Timothy 5:19), and exposed when guilty: "Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear." (1 Timothy 5:20) No witch hunt, and no cover-up. The same standard cuts both ways. And then the verse that should slow every church board and every quick opinion: "I charge thee before God... that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality." (1 Timothy 5:21) Nothing by partiality. No favorites. No protecting the man we like and crushing the man we don't. Paul even warns against rushing the very thing this letter is about, leadership: "Lay hands suddenly on no man." (1 Timothy 5:22) Slow down. Some men's sins are obvious and some are hidden, and time tells the truth that haste cannot. "Some men's sins are open beforehand, going before to judgment; and some men they follow after." (1 Timothy 5:24)

**The family that bleeds before it spends**
Why all this attention to widows and wages and witnesses and partiality? Because justice is what love looks like when it is organized. Anyone can love a church in the abstract. The test is whether the church does right by the people the world overlooks, and does it without favoritism, without rashness, without making the rules bend toward the people we happen to prefer. Paul told the Galatians the order of it: "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith." (Galatians 6:10) The household first, and then everyone.

This is the gospel made practical, and it traces back to the same mediating mercy under everything in the letter. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and he did it for people who could not pay him back, who had nothing to offer, who could never balance the account. The church that learned its life from a Savior like that cannot then run itself on preference and self-protection. A people ransomed by grace they did not earn cannot hoard honor or play favorites. We honor the widow because we were the widow. We protect the overlooked because we were overlooked, and a man who owed us nothing crossed an infinite distance to find us.

So look at how your church treats the people who can do nothing for it. That is not the side issue. That is the gospel, audited.

Honor the church as family.

## Godliness With Contentment, and the Good Fight
*What the love of money does to a soul, and what to do instead*

**Text:** 1 Timothy 6:1–21 · **Supporting:** 1 Timothy 6:6–10; Matthew 6:24; Hebrews 13:5; Philippians 4:11

The letter has named false teaching that flatters, false holiness that forbids, and now Paul names the engine running under so much of it. Money. Not money as a neutral tool, but money as the thing a heart can come to love, and what that love does to a person on the way down. He ends the letter here because this is where churches and ministers most quietly go to die.

**Religion as a business plan**
Paul exposes a particular kind of teacher, and the description is uncomfortably current. They are "men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness." (1 Timothy 6:5) Supposing that gain is godliness. They had turned the faith into a revenue model, godliness as a means to get. And Paul agrees that godliness is enormously profitable, then redefines the profit until the whole scheme collapses. "But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out." (1 Timothy 6:6–7)

There is the math that undoes the greed. You came in with nothing. You leave with nothing. Everything in between is on loan. The man chasing more is chasing something he cannot keep past his last breath, and he knows it, and he chases anyway. "And having food and raiment let us be therewith content." (1 Timothy 6:8) Contentment is not the absence of ambition. It is a soul that has stopped requiring more in order to be at rest. Paul learned it the hard way and said so: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." (Philippians 4:11) Learned. It does not come naturally. It is trained, like the godliness of chapter four.

**The root, and what it does to the one holding it**
Then comes the verse everyone half-quotes and few feel. "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows." (1 Timothy 6:10) Read what it actually does. It does not just compromise a man's ethics. It pierces him through. The love of money is a blade the man drives into his own soul, and the wound is *many sorrows*. He thinks he is acquiring security and he is impaling himself. And notice, it is not money that is the root. It is the love of it. The desire that has become a master.

Jesus said it cannot be shared. "No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon." (Matthew 6:24) Not *should not*. *Cannot.* It is a question of which throne is occupied, and money is a god that demands the whole seat. This is the false teachers' real disease. They were not preaching for the love of souls. They were preaching for the love of money, and they had pierced themselves through and mistaken the bleeding for blessing.

I have wanted the gospel to pay me, in money, in standing, in the security of being needed. The instinct that turned those Ephesian teachers into hucksters is not foreign to the man in the pulpit. It is the pulpit's particular temptation. Paul is not describing strangers. He is describing what I am capable of becoming.

**Flee, follow, fight, and guard**
So Paul charges the rich, and he does not tell them to feel guilty. He tells them to be generous. "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God... that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate." (1 Timothy 6:17–18) The cure for the love of money is not poverty. It is open hands. Generosity is what breaks the grip, because you cannot worship a god you keep giving away.

And then, to the minister, four verbs that close the letter like a drumbeat. "But thou, O man of God, flee these things; and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, meekness. Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life." (1 Timothy 6:11–12) Flee. Follow. Fight. Lay hold. Run from the love of gain. Chase the things that last. Treat the faith as a battle, not a business. And underneath it all, the last command of the letter: "O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust." (1 Timothy 6:20) Guard the deposit. The gospel was handed to you. It is not yours to sell, soften, or trade for gain. It is yours to keep and to hand on intact.

Hear how the whole letter closes its loop. It opened with a blasphemer saved by mercy and it ends with a minister told to flee greed and fight for faith, and both stand on the same ground. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. He did not come to make us rich. He gave himself a ransom, and the man who has been ransomed by that kind of love has been set free from needing to grab. God himself made the promise that pulls the love of money out by the root: "Be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee." (Hebrews 13:5) If you have him, you have the one thing that cannot be lost, and you are released from clawing after the things that can.

So the question the letter leaves on the table is the one it has been asking all along, only now it is sharpest. What are you guarding? The deposit, or the bank account. Because you will fight for one of them with your life, and only one of them will still be standing when you carry nothing out.

Flee greed. Fight for faith.
